text: A 'prop' is like a package being delivered from a parent component to a child. In React, these are the attributes you see inside a component's tag. Look at the <Profile /> tag in the code. What is the name of the 'package' (prop) being passed to it?
incorrectMessage: Not quite. Look for the text immediately to the left of the equals sign (=) inside the Profile tag. That's the prop's name!
correctMessage: That's right! The prop is called 'profileData'. Just like a function argument, it allows the parent to share specific information with the child.

text: Great! Now, if 'profileData' is the package, which component is the 'recipient' actually opening and using that package?
incorrectMessage: Look at the tag where the prop is defined. The name of the tag tells you which component is receiving that data.
correctMessage: Exactly! The Profile component receives the prop. It can now use that data to decide what to show on the screen.

text: In React, props always flow 'downhill' from a sender to a recipient. Looking at the code, which component is the 'sender' responsible for passing that profileData down to the Profile component?
incorrectMessage: Close! Look at which component's 'return' statement contains the <Profile /> tag. That outer component is the sender.
correctMessage: Nice work! App is the 'Parent' sender. This demonstrates 'One-Way Data Flow': data moves from App down to its children, never the other way around automatically.

text: Here's a tricky one: Props are 'read-only' (immutable) for the child. If the Profile component wanted to change its own 'profileData' and send it back up to App, can it do that using props alone? (Yes/No)
incorrectMessage: Remember the rules: props are like a one-way street. A child can look at the package it received, but it can't send a package back up the same way.
correctMessage: Right! Props are immutable for the child. To send info 'up', a parent must pass a special 'callback function' as a prop for the child to call.

text: Imagine we update the code to: <Profile profileData={profileData} theme='dark' />. How many total 'packages' (props) is Profile receiving now?
incorrectMessage: Count the labels before the equals signs. Each unique name={value} pair is an individual prop.
correctMessage: Spot on. It now receives two: 'profileData' and 'theme'. You're getting the hang of how data scales!

text: We've talked about props being 'packages.' In React, we also have 'State,' which is data managed *inside* a component. If a component wants to change its own data, should it use props or state?
incorrectMessage: Think back: props are 'read-only' and come from the parent. If a component needs to change its own internal data, it needs its own state!
correctMessage: Spot on! State is for internal, mutable data. Props are for external, handed-down data. Distinguishing the two is a major React milestone.

text: True or False: A child component can directly 'rename' or 'reassign' a prop it received from its parent.
incorrectMessage: Remember the rule of Immutability: Props are read-only. The child can use them, but it cannot change them!
correctMessage: Correct! This is a core part of React's design. Props are immutable for the child; only the parent who 'owns' the data can change it.

text: Look at the Navbar component in the code. Does it currently have any props being passed to it? (Yes/No)
incorrectMessage: Check the <Navbar /> tag. Do you see any name={value} pairs inside it like you do for the Profile component?
correctMessage: Exactly. Navbar is currently a 'Stateless' component that doesn't receive any data. Not every component needs props to function!

text: If we wanted the Navbar to display the user's name, where would that 'name' prop likely come from: the Navbar itself or its parent (App)?
incorrectMessage: Think about the delivery analogy. If a component needs a 'package' of data from the outside, who has to send it?
correctMessage: Right again! The parent (App) would provide the data as a prop. The child (Navbar) just receives and displays it.

text: In the code <Profile profileData={profileData} />, the part inside the curly braces `{profileData}` represents the actual data value. What is the name of the prop itself?
incorrectMessage: In name={value}, the name is on the left. In this specific case, they happen to share the same name!
correctMessage: Perfect. You can distinguish between the prop 'name' and the data 'value'. You are ready to move on to visualizing these relationships in a Tree Diagram!
